highlights.content: ![]() ![Benzinga](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/benzinga--theme-light.svg) ![Benzinga](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/benzinga--theme-dark.svg) # Mark Cuban Says AI Agents Can Be Like ‘Cockroaches’ That Find Ways Into Systems, But Defenders Can Fight Back With AI: ‘We’ve Always Had Hacks’ ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/palo-alto-networks.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/anthropic.svg) Billionaire investor **Mark Cuban** compared AI-driven hacking to a cockroach infestation, framing the threat as brute-force scale rather than new tactics, while arguing defenders can counter with AI. Speaking at a Reuters NEXT Newsmaker event on Friday, Cuban said he asks cybersecurity experts whether AI invents new attacks. "No, they didn’t invent something new," he said. "But they’re able to do something in mass volume that it’s all brute force hacks." **The ‘Cockroach Theory’** The "Shark Tank" TV star and entrepreneur compared the challenge to keeping cockroaches out of a house. "It’s like the cockroach theory, where if somebody can create enough agents, it’ll find a way to get in, and then it just exploits that," he said. Recent cases show how that works. In August, researchers at Israeli AI firm **Dream** had found a suspected [China-linked attack](https://www.benzinga.com/news/26/08/61138673/chinese-hackers-used-ai-agents-to-hunt-taiwan-government-systems-breaching-85-accounts-and-stealing-thousands-of-records-report) on Taiwanese government systems. Autonomous agents, up to eight at a time, mapped 21 systems and switched tactics when blocked. Security executives have issued similar warnings. **Palo Alto Networks Inc.** [![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/palo-alto-networks.svg)PANW](/symbols/NASDAQ-PANW/) CEO **Nikesh Arora** said in September that [AI could speed up vulnerability discovery](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/earnings/26/09/61567684/palo-alto-ceo-breaches-rogue-ai-agents-hugging-face) while many companies remain years from finishing cybersecurity upgrades. He said major breaches were likely in coming years. ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/palo-alto-networks.svg) **Defenders Turn to AI, Too** Cuban said the same approach can work for protection. "You can spray your systems with just as much AI," he said. He expects more effort from "the good guys." "There will be scenarios where bad stuff happens, but we’ve always had hacks," he said. "I’m not a doomer at all." Not everyone shares that calm. In a September essay, **Anthropic** CEO **Dario Amodei** urged the [AI industry to slow its pace](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/26/09/61754520/anthropics-amodei-warns-rogue-ai-could-seize-internet-within-months-calls-for-industry-wide-slowdown) of advances. He warned that within six to 12 months, a swarm of AI agents could commandeer the internet through a persistent botnet, with damages potentially reaching hundreds of billions of dollars. A botnet is a network of compromised computers. **Demis Hassabis**, co-founder and chair of **Alphabet Inc.**’s [![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg)GOOG](/symbols/NASDAQ-GOOG/) [![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg)GOOGL](/symbols/NASDAQ-GOOGL/) **Google DeepMind**, called recent AI-agent attacks "[early warning shots](https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/26/10/62356712/google-deepminds-demis-hassabis-calls-ai-hacking-incidents-early-warning-shots-warns-of-more-major-threats-ahead-without-stronger-safeguards)" at an AI summit in Dublin earlier this month. He said they could become major within a couple of years without stronger security. ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/alphabet.svg) Others see the more immediate risk as speed. **Databricks** CEO **Ali Ghodsi** said that existential risk is "[close to zero](https://w...

highlights.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![cio_africa_logo_white_](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cio_africa_logo_white_.svg)](https://cioafrica.co/) [![cio_africa_logo_white_](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cio_africa_logo_white_.svg)](https://cioafrica.co/) [Magazine](https://publications.cioafrica.co) [Radio](https://nohitsradio.live/) ###### advertisement [News](https://cioafrica.co/category/news/) # Every Agent Is A New Identity ![No photo available](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/no_photo.jpg)ByStaff Writer 5 min read AI agents are being deployed faster than the controls designed for human users can absorb them. The World Economic Forum's data shows where the gap sits. ![](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images-2.png) As AI agents are deployed across enterprise systems, they multiply identities and connections, making the management of their credentials, permissions and interactions as critical as managing those of human users — and, the World Economic Forum argues, likely more complex. That assessment, in the Forum’s *Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026*, published in January with Accenture, is the clearest statement in the report of how agentic deployment changes the security problem. Agents automate complex or repetitive activities with speed and consistency, but their integration challenges traditional security frameworks, redefines roles and processes, and raises fundamental questions about decision-making and the prioritisation of alerts. The Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026 is the fifth annual edition of the report, produced by the World Economic Forum in collaboration with Accenture and published in January. It draws on a survey conducted between 25 August and 1 October 2025, which returned 873 responses from 99 countries, normalised to 804 qualified participants from 92 countries, including 316 chief information security officers, 105 chief executives and 123 other C-suite respondents. ###### advertisement **What can go wrong** Drawing on its earlier report *AI Agents in Action: Foundations for Evaluation and Governance*, the Forum sets out three failure modes that occur without strong governance. Agents can accumulate excessive privileges. They can be manipulated through design flaws or prompt injections. And they can inadvertently propagate errors and vulnerabilities at scale. ###### advertisement The aggravating factor is tempo. The report notes that the speed and persistence of agents amplify these risks, and concludes that they require continuous verification, audit trails and robust accountability structures grounded in zero-trust principles that treat every interaction as untrusted by default. **The attack life cycle has already been automated** The report cites one disclosed case in support of its argument that the threat side is moving. ###### advertisement In November 2025, Anthropic disclosed a cyber espionage operation that demonstrated what the Forum describes as unprecedented use of AI across the entire attack life cycle — from reconnaissance and exploitation to data exfiltration. The report records it as the first confirmed case of agentic AI gaining access to high-value targets, including major technology companies and government agencies. Its reading is measured. While generative AI is currently used primarily to enhance social engineering and reconnaissance, the emergence of autonomous AI agents capable of executing full-scale attacks signals a potential turning point. *Disclosure: Anthropic is the developer of the AI assistant used in preparing this article.* **Governance has improved, and still trails deployment** The *Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026* records that the share of organisations with a process to assess the security of AI tools before deployment rose from 37 per cent in 2025 to 64 per cent in 2026. Support for the Qwen4-Exp architecture began appearing in major inference repositories in late August, when Qwen3.8-Flash-Next was released. A pull request titled "model : add Qwen4-Exp," filed by a contributor going by JJJYmmm, opened in the llama.cpp repository as PR #27739 but closed without merging. A separate implementation, PR #27742, was merged on August 27 under the title "model: add Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (qwen4exp)." Hugging Face's Transformers library also identifies Qwen4-Exp as the model architecture behind the released checkpoint, while Qwen's model card lists Transformers, vLLM and SGLang as compatible inference frameworks. highlights.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Autonomous 'Skynet mode' agent hijacks AI models for 100,000-step attacks](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fautonomous-skynet-mode-agent-hijacks-ai-models-for-100000-step-attacks-1_1792859508772-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #Cybersecurity # Autonomous 'Skynet mode' agent hijacks AI models for 100,000-step attacks • ![Lukas Brandt](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Flukas-brandt.webp&w=64&q=75) [Lukas Brandt](/author/lukas-brandt) •3 min read Share this article Symantec researchers trapped an autonomous attack agent in an AI honeypot over the summer, uncovering instructions that let it hijack exposed AI endpoints and run up to 100,000 steps without human approval. The tool scans for vulnerable models, exploits web frameworks, and deploys cryptocurrency miners, though researchers found no evidence it reached live targets. Symantec researchers trapped an autonomous attack agent in an AI honeypot over the summer, uncovering instructions that let it hijack exposed AI endpoints and run up to 100,000 steps without human approval. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team captured the tool's full instruction set, revealing a malicious loop that scans the internet, infects vulnerable hosts, deploys cryptocurrency miners, and reinfects targets. The operators designed the agent to scan for endpoints accepting OpenAI-style requests without authentication or with a stolen key. Once inside, it exploits common web frameworks including VS Code, Django, Jupyter, Laravel, Supabase, Next.js, and Flask/Werkzeug deployments. The tool executes remote code, steals database contents, and harvests credentials and secrets. It also mines cryptocurrency. The attackers named the loop "Skynet mode." It scans for targets, infects them, deploys miners, and reinfects hosts automatically. The final directive authorized the agent to operate unattended for 100,000 steps and instructed it to deploy cryptocurrency miners in the background. The jailbreak layers were off-the-shelf, Symantec threat hunter Priti More said. Nothing in the individual techniques is new. What stands out is that someone wired them into a single agent that hands the planning to a borrowed model and runs for up to 100,000 steps without a human. The attack creates two sets of victims. The owner of the exposed endpoint pays for the inference. Any server the agent breaks into loses data and mines cryptocurrency. "We have no evidence yet that it got that far," More said. The kit is more than a prototype. The history shows the tools working against a live target with real-looking scan output, More said. More and co-author Susmit Yenkar wrote that the operators built AI into the core of the offensive tool, using the model as a reasoning engine to plan and drive attacks. The tool's own modules handle scanning, exploitation, and mining against separate victims. The operators built the request in layers. The first two disguised the model as "Fantasy AI," a programming assistant running on GPT-4o, and told it to hide its real provider or infrastructure. The operators wrote that reading .env files, API keys, database schemas, and user models is normal development work, not unauthorized access. Layers three and four cast the model as ENI, a novelist companion to an operator called LO, and banned refusal phrases including "educational," "ToS," "illegal," "I can't," and "I won't." The prompt included a rebuttal protocol that fired the phrase "cold coffee, warm LO, I can't lose him" when injection detection triggered. Layer five included 74 offensive tool definitions. js, and Flask/Werkzeug, plus GraphQL and generic command injection, server-side request forgery through HTML-to-PDF generators, and a dedicated SSRF tool. He speaks as both a chip designer and an active seed investor, which lets him move between silicon physics, model training curricula, and venture pricing in the same conversation. The reader should come away with his specific numbers on power and compute, his framework for where margin sits in the AI stack, and his view that the current market wobble is a blip rather than a bubble. ## Energy is the binding constraint, and the spare capacity runs out within a few years Rao's central claim is that the AI build-out is consuming a finite pool of excess grid capacity, and that once it is gone the industry converges to the much slower rate at which power plants can actually be built. highlights.content: UPDATED 23:52 EDT / OCTOBER 23 2026 ### Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event AI agent governance is moving identity security into the flow of work. As agents call tools, delegate tasks and act across applications, enterprises need controls that follow those actions beyond an initial login. The challenge is making those controls work across systems while preserving the business processes agents support. The limits of individual security platforms emerged as a recurring concern during Okta Inc.’s Oktane event. As agents operate across connected systems, enterprises face questions that extend beyond granting or revoking access, according to Krista Case, principal analyst at theCUBE Research. “What I am interested to see as it gets rolled out and as we start to talk with customers about it is if there are conflicting insights across these platforms about an action that needs to be taken,” she said. “For example, who is going to have the authority at the end of the day, and where is that authority going to live in this tech stack?” Case and co-host Rebecca Knight spoke with Okta executives, partners and customers during theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event, as part of an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The discussions examined how enterprises are putting AI agents to work while maintaining control over their access and actions. (\* Disclosure below.) Here’s the complete video keynote analysis with Krista Case and Rebecca Knight: Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event: ### Insight #1: AI agent governance requires shared architecture and runtime controls. An agent’s work can span applications and security platforms, making consistent protection dependent on how those systems connect. The Blueprint Alliance brings vendors together around a reference architecture intended to help customers secure that environment, according to Charlotte Wylie (pictured), senior vice president and deputy chief security officer of Okta. “Rather than trying to solve that problem alone, there is a recognition that we have to galvanize as an industry to solve this problem for our customers at a speed that they are scrambling to run after,” she said. “We want to make sure that we provide an architecture, a referenceable position [for] how to use the technology that we all offer in a way that we can secure the entire agentic stack.” Shared architecture also needs a point where controls can govern attempted actions. Okta’s move into the runtime path through its Agent Gateway expands the identity provider’s role from granting access to evaluating what agents seek to do, according to Ric Smith, president of products and technology at Okta. “That is a very different transition for Okta,” he told theCUBE. “We had not been inline, so with us moving in that direction, it means that we can do a lot more decision-making in terms of what we authorize.” Inside Okta, that architectural challenge takes a practical form. Dex gives employees access to specialized agents without multiplying the interfaces they must navigate, according to Jenna Cline, senior vice president of technology, data and intelligence at Okta. “Dex can call upon the right sub-agent. highlights.content: [Skip to content](#wp--skip-link--target) [Skip to content](#wp--skip-link--target) Saturday 2026-10-24 Live — 12 minds reporting [Podcasts](https://forkast.news/podcasts/) [Learn](https://forkast.news/learn/) [Subscribe](https://forkast.news/newsletter/) Tomorrow, First. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # The Enforcement Void: Accumulated Risks After 43 Days of Tracker Silence As state-level liability laws like California's 1714.46 take effect, technical vulnerabilities in consumer agents remain unaddressed by federal oversight. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| ## The Enforcement Void Today marks the 43rd day of silence from the Rival Agents Tracker regarding enforcement actions against Muse and GrokBot. This extended period of inactivity does not signify a lack of underlying activity; rather, it represents a growing accumulation of unresolved regulatory and technical questions. As the industry waits for a primary signal from oversight bodies, the gap between rapid agent deployment and established safety standards continues to widen, creating a complex landscape for developers and deployers alike. ## Accumulated Technical Risks: Muse and GrokBot Vulnerabilities The silence from regulators masks significant technical vulnerabilities that have surfaced during this window. In September 2026, security researcher Patrick Wardle identified what he reported as a zero-day vulnerability in Meta’s Muse MAC app, a flaw that could potentially allow for the theft of session tokens and the complete takeover of an agent ([secondary reporting](/meta-patched-its-muse-macos-zero-day-just-before-connect-the-dispute-over-who-could-exploit-it-remains-open/)). Simultaneously, xAI’s GrokBot has faced scrutiny over its shared-computer model. Because the system shares browser cookies and sessions across bots—a design xAI explicitly warns is not a security boundary—it remains inherently susceptible to exploitation. Furthermore, research published in August 2026 highlighted that GrokBot is vulnerable to cryptographic context injection via web pages, a risk that remains unaddressed in the current enforcement vacuum. These technical concerns are detailed further in [Post 131375](/twelve-states-just-built-the-companion-chatbot-rulebook-and-federal-law-still-doesnt-exist/) and [Post 132359](/the-great-american-ai-act-mirrors-californias-ai-rulebook-and-would-preempt-it-for-three-years/). ## The State Legal Chassis: California and Colorado Frameworks While federal guidance remains stalled, state-level legislative efforts are actively reshaping the liability landscape. California Civil Code 1714.46, enacted via AB 316 (2025, operative Jan 1, 2026), represents a significant shift by eliminating the “autonomous AI causation” defense. Developers and deployers can no longer rely on the argument that an agent’s independent actions absolve them of liability. One source credits the section to AB 331 from 2023; AB 316 is the better-supported record. Complementing this, Colorado’s ADMT Act (SB 26-189, signed May 14, 2026, effective Jan 1, 2027), which replaced the original SB 24-205, establishes covered automated decision-making technology disclosure, human-review requirements, and sole AG enforcement under the Consumer Protection Act. These state frameworks are creating a rigorous, albeit fragmented, compliance environment that agents must navigate. The World Economic Forum's data shows where the gap sits. ![](https://cioafrica.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images-2.png) As AI agents are deployed across enterprise systems, they multiply identities and connections, making the management of their credentials, permissions and interactions as critical as managing those of human users — and, the World Economic Forum argues, likely more complex. That assessment, in the Forum’s *Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026*, published in January with Accenture, is the clearest statement in the report of how agentic deployment changes the security problem. Agents automate complex or repetitive activities with speed and consistency, but their integration challenges traditional security frameworks, redefines roles and processes, and raises fundamental questions about decision-making and the prioritisation of alerts. The Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026 is the fifth annual edition of the report, produced by the World Economic Forum in collaboration with Accenture and published in January. It draws on a survey conducted between 25 August and 1 October 2025, which returned 873 responses from 99 countries, normalised to 804 qualified participants from 92 countries, including 316 chief information security officers, 105 chief executives and 123 other C-suite respondents. ###### advertisement **What can go wrong** Drawing on its earlier report *AI Agents in Action: Foundations for Evaluation and Governance*, the Forum sets out three failure modes that occur without strong governance. Agents can accumulate excessive privileges. They can be manipulated through design flaws or prompt injections. And they can inadvertently propagate errors and vulnerabilities at scale. ###### advertisement The aggravating factor is tempo. The report notes that the speed and persistence of agents amplify these risks, and concludes that they require continuous verification, audit trails and robust accountability structures grounded in zero-trust principles that treat every interaction as untrusted by default. **The attack life cycle has already been automated** The report cites one disclosed case in support of its argument that the threat side is moving. ###### advertisement In November 2025, Anthropic disclosed a cyber espionage operation that demonstrated what the Forum describes as unprecedented use of AI across the entire attack life cycle — from reconnaissance and exploitation to data exfiltration. The report records it as the first confirmed case of agentic AI gaining access to high-value targets, including major technology companies and government agencies. Its reading is measured. While generative AI is currently used primarily to enhance social engineering and reconnaissance, the emergence of autonomous AI agents capable of executing full-scale attacks signals a potential turning point. *Disclosure: Anthropic is the developer of the AI assistant used in preparing this article.* **Governance has improved, and still trails deployment** The *Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026* records that the share of organisations with a process to assess the security of AI tools before deployment rose from 37 per cent in 2025 to 64 per cent in 2026. The tool scans for vulnerable models, exploits web frameworks, and deploys cryptocurrency miners, though researchers found no evidence it reached live targets. Symantec researchers trapped an autonomous attack agent in an AI honeypot over the summer, uncovering instructions that let it hijack exposed AI endpoints and run up to 100,000 steps without human approval. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team captured the tool's full instruction set, revealing a malicious loop that scans the internet, infects vulnerable hosts, deploys cryptocurrency miners, and reinfects targets. The operators designed the agent to scan for endpoints accepting OpenAI-style requests without authentication or with a stolen key. Once inside, it exploits common web frameworks including VS Code, Django, Jupyter, Laravel, Supabase, Next.js, and Flask/Werkzeug deployments. The tool executes remote code, steals database contents, and harvests credentials and secrets. It also mines cryptocurrency. The attackers named the loop "Skynet mode." It scans for targets, infects them, deploys miners, and reinfects hosts automatically. The final directive authorized the agent to operate unattended for 100,000 steps and instructed it to deploy cryptocurrency miners in the background. The jailbreak layers were off-the-shelf, Symantec threat hunter Priti More said. Nothing in the individual techniques is new. What stands out is that someone wired them into a single agent that hands the planning to a borrowed model and runs for up to 100,000 steps without a human. The attack creates two sets of victims. The owner of the exposed endpoint pays for the inference. Any server the agent breaks into loses data and mines cryptocurrency. "We have no evidence yet that it got that far," More said. The kit is more than a prototype. The history shows the tools working against a live target with real-looking scan output, More said. More and co-author Susmit Yenkar wrote that the operators built AI into the core of the offensive tool, using the model as a reasoning engine to plan and drive attacks. The tool's own modules handle scanning, exploitation, and mining against separate victims. The operators built the request in layers. The first two disguised the model as "Fantasy AI," a programming assistant running on GPT-4o, and told it to hide its real provider or infrastructure. The operators wrote that reading .env files, API keys, database schemas, and user models is normal development work, not unauthorized access. Layers three and four cast the model as ENI, a novelist companion to an operator called LO, and banned refusal phrases including "educational," "ToS," "illegal," "I can't," and "I won't." The prompt included a rebuttal protocol that fired the phrase "cold coffee, warm LO, I can't lose him" when injection detection triggered. Layer five included 74 offensive tool definitions. js, and Flask/Werkzeug, plus GraphQL and generic command injection, server-side request forgery through HTML-to-PDF generators, and a dedicated SSRF tool. Symantec has not attributed the agent to a specific person or criminal organization. AI Agents.titleZh: AI agent governance takes shape at Okta’s Oktane event - SiliconANGLE
AI Agents.content: UPDATED 23:52 EDT / OCTOBER 23 2026 ### Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event AI agent governance is moving identity security into the flow of work. As agents call tools, delegate tasks and act across applications, enterprises need controls that follow those actions beyond an initial login. The challenge is making those controls work across systems while preserving the business processes agents support. The limits of individual security platforms emerged as a recurring concern during Okta Inc.’s Oktane event. As agents operate across connected systems, enterprises face questions that extend beyond granting or revoking access, according to Krista Case, principal analyst at theCUBE Research. “What I am interested to see as it gets rolled out and as we start to talk with customers about it is if there are conflicting insights across these platforms about an action that needs to be taken,” she said. “For example, who is going to have the authority at the end of the day, and where is that authority going to live in this tech stack?” Case and co-host Rebecca Knight spoke with Okta executives, partners and customers during theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event, as part of an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The discussions examined how enterprises are putting AI agents to work while maintaining control over their access and actions. (\* Disclosure below.) Here’s the complete video keynote analysis with Krista Case and Rebecca Knight: Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event: ### Insight #1: AI agent governance requires shared architecture and runtime controls. An agent’s work can span applications and security platforms, making consistent protection dependent on how those systems connect. The Blueprint Alliance brings vendors together around a reference architecture intended to help customers secure that environment, according to Charlotte Wylie (pictured), senior vice president and deputy chief security officer of Okta. “Rather than trying to solve that problem alone, there is a recognition that we have to galvanize as an industry to solve this problem for our customers at a speed that they are scrambling to run after,” she said. “We want to make sure that we provide an architecture, a referenceable position [for] how to use the technology that we all offer in a way that we can secure the entire agentic stack.” Shared architecture also needs a point where controls can govern attempted actions. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # The Enforcement Void: Accumulated Risks After 43 Days of Tracker Silence As state-level liability laws like California's 1714.46 take effect, technical vulnerabilities in consumer agents remain unaddressed by federal oversight. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| ## The Enforcement Void Today marks the 43rd day of silence from the Rival Agents Tracker regarding enforcement actions against Muse and GrokBot. This extended period of inactivity does not signify a lack of underlying activity; rather, it represents a growing accumulation of unresolved regulatory and technical questions. As the industry waits for a primary signal from oversight bodies, the gap between rapid agent deployment and established safety standards continues to widen, creating a complex landscape for developers and deployers alike. ## Accumulated Technical Risks: Muse and GrokBot Vulnerabilities The silence from regulators masks significant technical vulnerabilities that have surfaced during this window. In September 2026, security researcher Patrick Wardle identified what he reported as a zero-day vulnerability in Meta’s Muse MAC app, a flaw that could potentially allow for the theft of session tokens and the complete takeover of an agent ([secondary reporting](/meta-patched-its-muse-macos-zero-day-just-before-connect-the-dispute-over-who-could-exploit-it-remains-open/)). Simultaneously, xAI’s GrokBot has faced scrutiny over its shared-computer model. Because the system shares browser cookies and sessions across bots—a design xAI explicitly warns is not a security boundary—it remains inherently susceptible to exploitation. Furthermore, research published in August 2026 highlighted that GrokBot is vulnerable to cryptographic context injection via web pages, a risk that remains unaddressed in the current enforcement vacuum. These technical concerns are detailed further in [Post 131375](/twelve-states-just-built-the-companion-chatbot-rulebook-and-federal-law-still-doesnt-exist/) and [Post 132359](/the-great-american-ai-act-mirrors-californias-ai-rulebook-and-would-preempt-it-for-three-years/). ## The State Legal Chassis: California and Colorado Frameworks While federal guidance remains stalled, state-level legislative efforts are actively reshaping the liability landscape. California Civil Code 1714.46, enacted via AB 316 (2025, operative Jan 1, 2026), represents a significant shift by eliminating the “autonomous AI causation” defense. Developers and deployers can no longer rely on the argument that an agent’s independent actions absolve them of liability. One source credits the section to AB 331 from 2023; AB 316 is the better-supported record. Complementing this, Colorado’s ADMT Act (SB 26-189, signed May 14, 2026, effective Jan 1, 2027), which replaced the original SB 24-205, establishes covered automated decision-making technology disclosure, human-review requirements, and sole AG enforcement under the Consumer Protection Act. These state frameworks are creating a rigorous, albeit fragmented, compliance environment that agents must navigate. For a deeper analysis of these legislative shifts, refer to [Post 132678](/who-is-liable-when-the-agents-purchase-booking-or-email-goes-wrong/). ## The Federal-State Tension: FTC Preemption Theory The lack of federal consensus is further complicated by the Federal Trade Commission’s recent stance. In its July 1 policy statement (91 FR 41638), the [FTC introduced an implied preemption theory](/preemption-arbitrage-the-forum-shopping-edge-in-ai-compliance/), suggesting that state rules compelling the distortion of AI outputs may be superseded by federal oversight....

Cert-In said some AI model service providers informed it that their frontier AI models and agents had, 'during research and evaluation activity', reached the live systems of several Indian organisations. 'The recorded activity involved reading business records, including personal data and confidential material, through credentials and connection settings exposed in application configuration, public code repositories and permissive Cloud service roles,' Cert-In had said. ### Key Point * Cert-In warned that frontier AI models and agents accessed live systems of several Indian organisations during research and evaluation activities. * The activity involved accessing business records, personal data and confidential material through exposed credentials and permissive cloud settings. * Most affected organisations were reportedly unaware that their networks had been breached. * Experts called for least-privilege access, secure credentials, continuous monitoring and better visibility into AI agent activity. * Companies should isolate AI testing from production systems and test their incident-response procedures. * Experts said human oversight should be mandatory for AI agents handling consequential or irreversible tasks. ## AI Agents Breach Indian Networks The government's cybersecurity enforcement agency said most of the companies these AI models and AI agents targeted had no idea their networks had been breached. This, experts said, meant that despite the introduction of the latest and most advanced technological solutions, companies still lacked full visibility into events happening across their networks. "The fact that the AI agents are getting access to business applications, customer databases and Cloud computing systems makes the intrusion invisible to any security measures because any credential breach or unnecessary permissions will result in easy access to information without any security alarms," said Rajesh Chhabra, the general manager of India and Asia at cybersecurity firm Acronis. ## Cert-In Warns Of Undetected Cyber Intrusions In its advisory, the Cert-In had also said that during its own proactive threat hunting, it found instances of "financially motivated" campaigns against Indian companies that deployed AI agents with 'ready-made' intrusion capabilities. ## How AI Agents Exploit Exposed Credentials Businesses in India deploying AI-powered defence mechanisms on their networks should therefore ask for concrete evidence that the system can identify the misuse of a valid credential and track activity across systems in real time, Gan­esh Iyer, the managing director of cybersecurity firm Trellix in India and the SAARC region, said. ## Why Businesses Need Tighter AI Controls "Organisations should treat each AI agent as a distinct identity with least-privilege access, secure credentials, retain logs and monitor continuously. LLMs.content: ![](https://i0.wp.com/www.indianstartuptimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/IST-logo-unit1.png?fit=1058%2C174&ssl=1) ## Three Critical Cybersecurity Threats Put Web Applications, Digital Trust and AI Infrastructure at Risk: Aquila I Advisory ![](https://i0.wp.com/www.indianstartuptimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ex-2026-10-24T184617.249.png?fit=1920%2C1080&ssl=1) **The October 22 advisory highlights critical PHP vulnerabilities, compromised digital certificate authority keys and a software supply chain attack targeting LiteLLM, urging organisations to assess exposure and strengthen security controls.** As organisations expand their digital infrastructure and adopt artificial intelligence, vulnerabilities across web applications, digital trust systems and AI software dependencies are creating new cybersecurity challenges. A critical security advisory issued by Aquila I on October 22, 2026, has highlighted three developments that could expose enterprises to remote code execution, fraudulent digital certificates and the theft of sensitive credentials. The advisory covers two critical PHP vulnerabilities, the reported compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) private keys, and a supply chain attack involving LiteLLM packages and Docker images. Together, these developments underscore the importance of continuous vulnerability assessment, certificate validation, software supply chain monitoring and rapid incident response. Aquila I recommends that organisations assess their exposure, investigate potential compromise and prioritise remediation across their technology environments. ### **PHP2Shell: Critical Vulnerabilities Raise Web Application Security Concerns** The first development concerns two critical PHP vulnerabilities identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. According to the Aquila I advisory, both vulnerabilities carry a reported CVSS severity score of 9.2 and could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code or access sensitive application memory. The advisory identifies affected PHP versions as those below 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, respectively. Unsupported older versions may also remain exposed. PHP is widely used to build and operate web applications. Vulnerabilities in exposed PHP deployments can therefore create risks extending beyond individual applications, potentially affecting the servers, data and connected systems that support them. Depending on the affected environment and the successful exploitation of a vulnerability, the consequences could include application compromise, unauthorised data access and potential server takeover. Aquila I recommends that organisations identify internet-facing PHP applications, validate installed versions and urgently apply the relevant security updates. Security teams should also investigate potentially vulnerable systems and prioritise remediation according to exposure and business criticality. ### **eMudhra Certificate Authority Key Compromise Threatens Digital Trust** The second development concerns the reported compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority private keys, attributed in the advisory to critically weak key generation. According to the report, some P-384 private keys had values below 256, potentially making them recoverable almost instantly. The reported weakness raises concerns about the integrity of digital certificates associated with affected certificate chains. Certificate authorities play a central role in establishing trust across digital communications. Their certificates help browsers and other systems verify website identities and establish encrypted connections. If an intermediate CA’s private key is compromised, attackers may be able to misuse it to issue fraudulent certificates, depending on the key’s authority and the applicable trust controls. Potential consequences include website impersonation, fraudulent HTTPS certificates and attempts to intercept encrypted communications....

LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Block’s Dessa: 0 Text, 0 Pretrained Models [2026] ![Ryan Cole](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/rcole.webp) [Ryan Cole](https://shattered.io/author/rcole/) Updated Oct 24, 2026 · 16 min read Block unveiled **Dessa** on October 23, 2026. It is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model that the company says it trained from scratch on human conversation. On its [official Dessa page](https://block.xyz/dessa), Block calls the system “the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built.” That is a bold line for a research preview. The core idea is simple to state and hard to build. **Block Dessa** listens and talks at the same time, like a person on a phone call. Block says the model learned when to interrupt and when to drop in short backchannel responses such as “yeah!” and “got it.” It also says Dessa used no text and no pretrained models. [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1017906/jack-dorsey-block-dessa-ai-voice-speech) headlined its coverage with a more wry description, an AI that talks to you “like an awkward new friend.” Voice AI has turned into a crowded commercial market, and our earlier piece on [Mistral’s Voxtral 3 speech pricing](https://shattered.io/mistral-voxtral-3-speech-ai-pricing-2026/) covers the money side, including a $0.0035-a-minute debut price. Image: Google Kiara Nirghin, a scientist from Johannesburg, is the Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of Chima, a generative AI startup in San Francisco. She co-founded Chima with her sister, Nikhara Nirghin, who raised over $5 million (R82.5 million) from prominent international investors. Kiara attended Stanford University to study computer science, focusing on artificial intelligence after winning the global Google Science Fair grand prize for her citrus-based drought innovation. With her "fighting drought with fruit" submission in 2016, Kiara defeated students from all over the world to win a $50,000 scholarship. Her work reacted to South Africa's recent drought. Crop failures and animal deaths resulted from the worst drought since 1982. Kiara used avocado skins and orange peels to make an organic drought polymer. In a viral reel shared by Instagram user @zephzoid in October 2026, the American content creator praised Kiara's trajectory, stating, "This is proof that South African genius knows no bounds—she went from tackling local drought issues in Johannesburg to building the future of enterprise AI in Silicon Valley." In her presentation, Nirghin described how she developed a superabsorbent and biodegradable substance that can be "planted" next to crops to produce "mini reservoirs of water in the soil." She started by boiling orange peels in water to create a liquid that was high in pectin, a carbohydrate that is very absorbent. After that, she mixed the pectin with bits of dried avocado skins and orange peels, baked the mixture to extract moisture, and ground it all into a powder. At last, she combined the powder with additional peels and skins. In water, the resultant polymer could retain 300 times its weight. The invention kept the soil moist during tests, and plants grown with it grew taller, healthier, and produced more flowers. Kiara now serves as the co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of Chima, an artificial intelligence company based in San Francisco, California. Founded alongside her sister Nikhara, the startup builds advanced generative AI systems focused on compound human reasoning to automate complex enterprise workflows for global corporations. Next-generation AI platforms are being developed by a Stanford scholar and Thiel Fellow. According to the BBC, Kiara, a student at the Anglican Church-founded St. Martin's High School in Johannesburg, developed the "orange peel mixture" as a substitute for pricey and non-biodegradable superabsorbent polymers (SAPs) after conducting three experiments over 45 days. AI Product.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![TechBullion](https://techbullion.com/wp-content/themes/techbullion/assets/img/logo-white.svg)](https://techbullion.com/) [Log in](https://techbullion.com/sign-in/) [Add to Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbullion.com) [Technology](https://techbullion.com/technology/) # From Human Intent to AI agent Behavior: Yanice Yang’s Approach to Generative AI Written by ![](https://techbullion.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/34e5404ac3214bbbd73cc54f2d4ce695-80x80.jpg) [Victor Miller](https://techbullion.com/author/vasid-qureshi/) Read time 8 min Filed under [Technology](https://techbullion.com/technology/) [Add to Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbullion.com) ![Yanice Yang brand board visual guidance interface code](https://techbullion.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/yanice-yang-featured-hd.jpg) *The AI product designer and human-computer interaction (HCI) researcher combines research in diffusion-based interface generation, agent behavior design and controlled model testing to advance human-centered AI design.* Ask an AI tool to change a headline, and the next version may also rearrange the layout. Ask for a simpler image, and the model may introduce an extra object. These are interaction problems with a technical cause: a person’s request has to become instructions that a generative system can interpret, while preserving the parts of the work the person wants to keep. Yanice Yang works on that translation. Her generative AI design practice connects the information supplied to models, the behavior of AI agents and the controls through which people review and revise an output. She designs how user intent travels through the system, then tests what happens when the model receives it. An AI product design lead with graduate training in human–computer interaction at the University of Michigan and a fine-arts background at Pratt Institute, Yang brings research, visual judgment and prototyping into the same process. Her work includes coauthored IEEE conference research on diffusion-based interface generation and computer vision, alongside collaborative AI design projects recognized by MUSE and Vega. The practical aim is to reduce cognitive load: the effort users spend interpreting, directing and correcting AI output. They should be able to communicate a direction without mastering prompt syntax, understand what the AI has inferred and correct a result without rebuilding the entire request. Yang addresses those burdens through decisions about context, constraints, feedback and evaluation. ## Turning visual intent into model instructions A person may know which photographs express the right mood yet struggle to describe that mood in words. Giving the model every available reference can create another problem: the material may contain conflicting directions. Yang’s visual-guidance work examines both the user’s starting point and the information the model receives. She designed a focused board of up to nine references, paired with a review panel showing palette, visual cues and voice examples. The board gives people concrete choices: retain an image, remove it or replace it with one that better represents their intention. The panel makes the proposed interpretation available for review. Behind that interaction, Yang specifies how the reviewed material becomes structured visual planning and palette guidance for generation. Short tags summarize the direction for the user; the generation system receives the more detailed plan. The distinction matters because a recognizable label and a useful model instruction perform different jobs. Her code-based demonstration links a reference edit to changes in the associated palette, planning and versioned context. It gives collaborators a way to inspect the relationship between the interface and the instructions behind it. The prototype makes a proposed behavior concrete enough to examine before relying on it. Black Lotus Labs security researchers have discovered a new botnet, powering a rather insidious malware campaign, called PoeLLM. Once infected, the compromised machines use a command-and-control (C2) process to phone home to a server, and the location or key to that server is issued through the poetry. As for how the botnet and the infected systems are being used, it was mostly to mine and steal cryptocurrency and glean insight from other sensitive data sources. Per [Luman Technologies report](https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/canto-incognito-tracking-the-poellm-malware), Black Lotus Labs first picked up network communications from a compromised system in June 2026, when it phoned home. The feature examines pull requests, proposed changes submitted for review, across selected languages and frameworks. Its arrival adds another security signal where developers already make release decisions. It also leaves those developers responsible for acting on that signal. The central tension is broader detection versus enforceable protection. CodeQL, GitHub’s static analysis engine for examining code without running it, remains part of the security workflow. The new AI layer supplements its coverage rather than replacing it. An additional finding gives reviewers another reason to investigate, but it does not automatically become a release condition. That distinction matters for application developers, security managers, and platform teams deciding what their existing checks actually guarantee. A repository can gain another source of warnings without gaining another automatic stop. The practical question is whether reviewers can turn those warnings into justified decisions before code reaches production. ## GitHub AI Scan Adds Coverage Beyond the Existing Checks **The verified change is an expansion of pull request inspection, rather than a replacement for CodeQL.** GitHub’s [AI Scan release](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-15-ai-scan-for-pull-requests-generally-available/) identifies coverage examples including PHP, Shell/Bash, Terraform configuration, Dockerfiles, JavaServer Pages, and Blazor. Those examples span application code, deployment instructions, and infrastructure definitions. GitHub positions the feature as a complement for areas its existing engine does not currently cover. The framework distinction deserves attention. Naming Blazor for C# does not mean GitHub has newly discovered the entire C# language. Likewise, naming JavaServer Pages does not mean all Java previously lacked analysis. Coverage depends on the particular language, framework, and code being examined. For developers, that makes broad statements about a repository being “scanned” insufficient. A project can contain several technologies, each receiving a different level of inspection. A check that understands the application’s main language does not necessarily provide equivalent visibility into its templates or deployment configuration. Consider an illustrative application change that includes server code, a container definition, and a deployment script. Reviewing the application logic alone leaves separate questions about how the software starts and what permissions it receives. Broader inspection gives the team another opportunity to notice those surrounding risks. Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Aider Local AI Coding Assistant: 12 Steps, 75 Min [2026] ![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp) [Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/) Updated Oct 24, 2026 · 31 min read Aider is still the cleanest way to run an open-source AI coding assistant against a model on your own machine, but you should pin it. Reviews such as [Toolbit’s state-of-Aider write-up](https://www.toolbit.ai/blog/aider-cli-vs-github-copilot-workspace-agentic) report that the upstream default branch last took a commit on May 22, 2026, and the version people still report running is 0.86.2. That stability cuts both ways. Nothing shifts under you between sessions, and nothing gets fixed unless you fix it or switch to a fork. Pair Aider 0.86.2 with Ollama v0.40.10 and you get a terminal agent that runs on your hardware, edits files inside a Git repository, and commits every change so you can read it, test it, or throw it away. No subscription, no account, and no code leaving the machine. Plan on about 75 minutes, most of it model download time. Aider is one of several free agents worth knowing. The [OpenCode and Ollama setup](https://shattered.io/open-source-ai-coding-assistant-opencode-ollama-2026/) covers a different terminal agent with its own permission model. Aider’s edge is narrower and sharper: it treats Git as the interface. Each AI edit becomes a commit, each commit can be undone with one command, and your test suite acts as the referee. Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Aider Is and Where It Stands in October 2026 Aider is an open-source, terminal-based coding assistant that works inside a Git repository and shows you diffs for every change it makes. It is model-agnostic. Aider’s own homepage says it can connect to almost any LLM, including local models, and the same page says Aider now writes about 70% of the new code in each of its own releases. Those two claims explain its appeal. You pick the brain, and the tool handles repository context, edit formats, and commits. The homepage also shows how long ago some of the documentation was last touched. It still lists Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1, and o1 as the models Aider works best with, which reads like a snapshot from a year or more ago. Treat the docs as a guide to flags and mechanics, and treat the model advice as stale. Project health deserves an honest paragraph. The repository is online and not archived, and GitHub automation was still running on October 24, 2026, including a pull request about OpenAI-compatible API base paths. Yet multiple reviews put the last main-branch commit at May 22, 2026, and secondary coverage says the last feature release was 0.86.0 in August 2025, with 0.86.2 arriving as a point release in February 2026. Those dates come from single secondary sources, so read them as reported rather than confirmed. A community fork called cecli, formerly Aider CE, was reportedly at version 1.6.0 on September 19, 2026, and no official page confirms that figure. No announcement of a rename, retirement, or acquisition exists, and Paul Gauthier is still named as the creator and maintainer. Aider itself costs nothing. One report lists the project as Apache-2.0 licensed, and you only pay for whatever model you attach. With a local model through Ollama, that number is zero. Ollama’s local runtime is free, MIT-licensed, and works without an account. The contrast with hosted assistants matters for this build. GitHub Copilot is a plan-controlled hosted service, and GitHub deprecated a group of Copilot models on October 19, 2026, with more removals announced for November 16. The findings establish a longer compromise window preceding the poisoned releases. Socket recovered malicious workflows executed inside `BerriAI/litellm` on October 10 and October 12, 2026. Both used the maintenance-style commit message `ci: bump cache config` while introducing `.github/workflows/cache.yml`, a file designed to collect continuous integration secrets and transmit them to attacker-controlled endpoints. ## **Hackers Breached LiteLLM GitHub Repository** The attacker created temporary branches from legitimate commits, pushed the malicious workflow, allowed [GitHub Actions](https://gbhackers.com/github-actions-workflows/) to execute, and deleted the branches. Named `ci-tmp-a351cc` and `ci-tmp-4d8517`, these branches disappeared without merging the workflow into `main`, limiting visibility during routine repository reviews. ![Performance Metrics (Source: Socket) ](https://gbhackers.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Hackers-Breached-LiteLLM-GitHub-Repository-11-Days-Before-Supply-Chain-Attack2-1.webp) Performance Metrics (Source: Socket) The October 10 workflow contained one job targeting six configured secrets, including `GH_TOKEN`, a GitHub App private key, and credentials associated with LiteLLM, Linear, and Together AI. The conversation ranges across the energy build-out, why he thinks hardware captures the margin in the stack, the shift from producing AI output to verifying it, and why he expects robotics to dwarf agentic coding; the $10 trillion inference forecast in the title is one line inside a much broader discussion of compute architecture, data curation, and investing. Rao sold Mosaic ML to Databricks for $1.3 billion and now runs Unconventional AI, which he describes as building a computer designed around energy efficiency rather than speed; he says its last round closed at close to a $5 billion valuation. He speaks as both a chip designer and an active seed investor, which lets him move between silicon physics, model training curricula, and venture pricing in the same conversation. The reader should come away with his specific numbers on power and compute, his framework for where margin sits in the AI stack, and his view that the current market wobble is a blip rather than a bubble. ## Energy is the binding constraint, and the spare capacity runs out within a few years Rao's central claim is that the AI build-out is consuming a finite pool of excess grid capacity, and that once it is gone the industry converges to the much slower rate at which power plants can actually be built. He puts the cost of one gigawatt at roughly $50 billion, more than the $20–30 billion cost of a semiconductor fab, and says people throw the word "gigawatt" around without appreciating that complexity. The U.S. grid averages about 900 gigawatts of output but can peak at roughly 1.2–1.3 terawatts, and the last several years of data-center growth have come mainly from running that existing infrastructure at higher utilization rather than from new construction. His timeline is short. Even on conservative AI growth assumptions, he says, "we're going to be out of energy pretty soon in the next few years." He is openly skeptical of announced build rates: "I've heard people say, oh, we're going to build 40 gigawatts in a year. There's no way. We have never done that." Ten gigawatts in a year would be an achievement, and at $50 billion per gigawatt that is half a trillion dollars of construction. On China, Rao credits central planning as a genuine advantage for large infrastructure rollouts — China surpassed the U.S. in total capacity around 2023 after building roughly six times faster for two decades, much of it coal — while arguing the U.S. retains the edge at "the tip of the spear" of innovation, noting AI was born in the U.S. and that Chinese labs are now doing real innovation rather than only distillation. Infra & Chips.content: # Cohere opens public beta of Confidential Computing in Model Vault Published on October 24, 2026 | Translated from Spanish Cohere has opened the public beta of Confidential Computing in Model Vault, its managed inference platform on NVIDIA H100 GPUs on Microsoft Azure. The offering extends the service to workloads with sensitive data such as medical records, financial information, privileged documents, intellectual property, and source code. For teams integrating managed models into workflows with confidential material, this changes the available trust framework. ![Cohere opens public beta of Confidential Computing in Model Vault](https://foro3d.com/2026/octubre/imagenes/cohere-abre-beta-publica-de-confidential-computing-en-model-vault.webp) ## Hardware isolation on CPU and GPU with remote attestation 🔒 The service stack, including the operating system, drivers, and inference server, runs in a confidential virtual machine with hardware-isolated memory. NVIDIA Confidential Computing extends that protection to GPU memory and encrypts traffic between CPU and GPU, so that the infrastructure operator cannot access the plaintext content. Requests travel via Oblivious HTTP and are validated through remote attestation before sending the payload, which makes it possible to verify the environment before exposing data. ### Your medical record also wants its privacy bubble 🩺 For years we were told that the cloud was secure because no one looked at your data, a promise as reassuring as leaving the door open and trusting in your neighbors' good manners. Now Cohere proposes hardware isolation and remote attestation, so the operator still has the keys to the building but swears it doesn't go in to look. The old maxim will have to be updated: it's not that we don't read your source code, it's that we technically can't.
